status_reasoning: The development of the fTIR optical method coupled with high-speed imaging and FlyWalker software is well-documented with technical specifications, validation data from 71 videos, and demonstrated capability to track footprints and body position at high temporal (4 ms) and spatial resolution. The method is reproducible as the software is freely available.

Step parameters for wild-type flies are comprehensively characterized with quantitative data showing speed-dependent relationships: stance duration decreases with speed while swing duration remains constant, step length and swing speed increase linearly with speed, and step period plateaus at ~60 ms above 30 mm/s. These findings are consistent with previous literature and supported by data from 71 videos spanning 7.2-44.7 mm/s.

Spatial parameters of footprint positioning are well-characterized showing that faster flies have straighter stance traces, more spatially restricted steps (lower footprint clustering), and tighter motor control at touchdown (AEP) versus liftoff (PEP). Speed-dependent changes in AEP/PEP positions are documented with statistical significance, though some functional interpretations (C53, C54) remain speculative.

The finding that flies use a continuum of gait patterns rather than discrete gait transitions is well-supported by quantitative gait index analysis across speeds. Data show tripod gait dominates at high speeds (~70% of time) while slower flies increasingly use tetrapod and noncanonical combinations, with gradual rather than abrupt transitions. This contrasts with vertebrate locomotion and is supported by comprehensive gait mapping data.

Instantaneous speed analysis reveals wave-like patterns with peak speeds at mid-stance and minimum speeds during gait transitions, consistent with previous observations in stick insects. The finding that speed variation decreases at slower speeds, suggesting more even power distribution, is supported by high temporal resolution data and aligns with biomechanical expectations.

Footprint alignment analysis reveals distinct patterns at slow (<20 mm/s), medium (20-34 mm/s), and fast (>34 mm/s) speeds, with abrupt transitions suggesting different motor control programs. The correlation between alignment and tripod index supports functional interpretations, and the underrepresentation of ~20 mm/s speeds in the dataset provides converging evidence for a possible gait transition at this speed.

Phase coordination analysis shows that contralateral legs maintain ~0.5 phase relationship in both slow and fast flies, consistent with established patterns. The finding that slower animals display higher phase variability and decreased intersegmental phase values is supported by quantitative radial plot analysis, though the biological significance requires further interpretation.

Genetic inactivation of leg sensory neurons (using nan36a mutants and 5-40leg>TNT) demonstrates that proprioceptive feedback is important but not absolutely required for coordinated walking. Both genotypes showed deficient step precision (increased step length, more jittery movement) but maintained largely normal gait parameters and interleg coordination, including the ability to execute tripod gait. This is a key finding supported by quantitative comparisons across multiple parameters.

Speed-dependent effects of sensory deprivation are well-documented, showing that defects are more pronounced in slow-walking flies (footprint alignment, stance duration, tripod index). The observation that sensory-deprived flies exhibit some characteristics of fast wild-type flies supports the interpretation that fast-walking flies are less dependent on sensory feedback, though this remains partially inferential.

The suggestion that flies use distinct neural programs at slow, medium, and fast speeds is inferred from multiple parameters showing transitions at ~20 and ~34 mm/s, but direct neural evidence is lacking. While footprint clustering, stance linearity, and alignment data show speed-dependent patterns, the claim of distinct neural programs requires electrophysiological or neural circuit manipulation data for full support.

The mechanistic interpretation that CPG-interneuron communication is sufficient for coordination when all legs are equally impaired is explicitly speculative. While the sensory deprivation data support that interleg coordination can occur without proprioceptive feedback, the specific role of interneurons versus other mechanisms has not been directly tested and requires additional experiments targeting interneuron function.

The hypothesis of a leading role for forelegs in forward locomotion is supported by observations that foreleg swing phase duration decreases more with speed and swing speed varies more linearly with average speed compared to other leg segments. This is consistent with previous findings in stick insects and represents a reasonable inference from the segment-specific data.

The underrepresentation of speeds at ~20 mm/s and the statistical analysis showing non-Gaussian outliers in the tails suggest possible gait transitions, but the dataset may reflect sampling bias rather than biological avoidance of these speeds. While the Shapiro-Wilk test shows overall normality (p=0.31), the interpretation of underrepresentation as evidence for gait transitions requires additional experimental validation with controlled speed manipulation.
